sections.h2: Where is Linn County, Iowa, and what towns does it include?
sections.html:
Linn County sits in eastern Iowa, with Cedar Rapids as both its county seat and its largest city. The county was created on December 21, 1837, as part of Wisconsin Territory, and the seat moved from Marion to Cedar Rapids after voters approved the change in 1919 (Wikipedia).

It covers 724.669 square miles, which makes it the tenth largest county in Iowa by area. Its neighbors are Benton, Buchanan, Cedar, Delaware, Iowa, Johnson and Jones counties. The 2020 census counted 230,299 residents, the second-highest total of any Iowa county.

A seller's first practical question is which assessor and which school or city services apply, and the answer can change from one side of a city line to the other.

sections.h2: What drives the Linn County economy?
sections.html:
Cedar Rapids anchors the county's economy, with aerospace, grain processing and trucking among its large employers. A 2024 city report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranks Collins Aerospace in the 5,000 to 9,999 employee range.

  • Employers in the 1,000 to 4,999 range include Aegon USA, the Cedar Rapids Community School District, the City of Cedar Rapids, Cedar Rapids Steel Transport, Kirkwood Community College, PepsiCo and UnityPoint Health-St. Luke's.
  • Grain processing directly provides about 4,000 jobs in the city, and a large Quaker Oats mill sits on the north side of downtown.
  • CRST, a trucking company, is based in Cedar Rapids, and Aegon has its U.S. headquarters there.
  • In February 2025 a $750 million data center by Quality Technology Services was announced.

Coe College and Mount Mercy University are the city's four-year colleges, and Kirkwood Community College is the area's two-year college.

sections.h2: How did the 2008 flood and 2020 derecho affect Linn County homes?
sections.html:
Both events left lasting marks on Cedar Rapids housing. The Cedar River reached a record 31.12 feet on June 13, 2008, and 1,126 city blocks flooded, with 561 blocks severely damaged. About 7,749 properties were evacuated, including 5,900 homes, and at least 1,300 properties had to be demolished.

On August 10, 2020, a derecho hit the county with sustained winds of 60 to 80 miles per hour and gusts of 110 or more. Most residential and commercial buildings in Cedar Rapids were damaged, along with 20 schools, and about 95 percent of the city lost power.

For a seller, that history means older Cedar Rapids houses may carry past repair work. Gathering permits, contractor invoices and insurance paperwork before you talk to a buyer saves time, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can take a house in its current condition.

sections.h2: Which office handles Linn County property assessments?
sections.html:
It depends on where the house is. The Linn County Assessor covers the county's real property, and Cedar Rapids has its own City Assessor. The table lists the offices a Linn County seller is most likely to contact.

OfficeRoleContact
Linn County AssessorValues real property; revalues every two years on odd-numbered years; assessment date January 1linn.iowaassessors.com
Cedar Rapids City AssessorValues property in Cedar Rapids; revalued every year500 15th Avenue SW, 319-286-5888
Linn County TreasurerCollects tax, runs the tax sale, handles redemptions935 Second St. SW, 319-892-5500
Board of ReviewHears assessment protests; five members appointed by the Conference BoardThrough the assessor's office

Neither assessor collects tax or sets the rate. The City Assessor's page says its office "does not collect taxes, calculate taxes nor determine tax rate," and the county assessor's page puts the focus on value, with taxing bodies setting budgets and levies. Public utilities and railroads are assessed by the Iowa Department of Revenue.

sections.h2: What is the Linn County property tax calendar?
sections.html:
Assessment is as of January 1, bills are paid in two halves, and protests are due in April. The Linn County Assessor's timeline and the statewide treasurers' calendar line up as follows.

DateEvent
January 1Assessment date
By April 1Assessors complete assessments and notify owners
April 2 to 25Informal assessor hearings can be requested
April 2 to 30Protests filed with the Board of Review
May 1 to 31Board of Review considers protests
October 1Final equalization orders issued
October 9 to 31Equalization protests to the board
September 30 and March 31First and second halves payable
Third Monday in JuneAnnual county tax sale of unpaid parcels

The Linn County Treasurer says spring payments must be postmarked by March 31 and fall payments by September 30. Delinquent installments carry interest of 1.5 percent per month.

sections.h2: How do I protest a Linn County assessment?
sections.html:
File a written protest with the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30 of the assessment year. The board cannot extend that deadline, except in a declared disaster area, where the filing period runs May 1 through June 5 (Iowa Code 441.37).

The statute allows five grounds:

  • The assessment is not equitable compared with like property in the taxing district.
  • The property is assessed for more than the value the law allows.
  • The property is not assessable, is exempt, or is misclassified.
  • There is an error in the assessment.
  • There is fraud or misconduct, which must be stated specifically.

An oral hearing is available only if you request it in writing when you file. One form can cover several parcels if the same grounds apply. After deciding, the board must send written notice of its action and the reasons.

sections.h2: How do I pay Linn County property tax?
sections.html:
You can pay online, by mail, in a drop box, by phone or in person at the Treasurer's office at 935 Second St. SW in Cedar Rapids. Checks go to the Linn County Treasurer, and the tax statement stub should go with the payment so it is credited correctly.

  • In-person cash and check payments carry no fee.
  • Online check payments cost $0.30, debit cards cost $3.25 plus $0.30 per transaction, and credit cards cost 2.20 percent plus $0.30 per transaction.
  • Online cash payments are not accepted.
  • Lobby hours are Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., with extended hours of 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on the second Wednesday of each month.

The Treasurer warns that USPS now postmarks mail by the day it is processed, not the day it is dropped off, so a late-processed envelope can be treated as late. A free manual postmark from a staffed retail counter avoids that.

sections.h2: What happens to Linn County property tax when I sell?
sections.html:
The tax stays with the property, so a sale has to account for any unpaid installments at closing. A closing agent splits the current installment under the purchase contract, and any delinquent amount is paid from proceeds so the buyer receives a clean title.

The Treasurer's office also prepares plat and mobile home clearances and processes tax suspensions, which can matter at closing. Iowa's transfer tax is 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, and the seller, as grantor, is the person liable (Iowa Code 428A.1 and 428A.3).

If taxes are far behind, the county can sell them at the June tax sale. The Treasurer conducts the sale, processes redemptions and issues tax sale deeds, and redemption of a sold parcel costs the sold amount plus 2 percent interest per month. Our statewide Iowa tax deed and tax lien sales guide covers the redemption steps. Cash Home Buyers buys Linn County houses as-is, including ones with tax issues, and we confirm numbers with you before any offer.

faqs.q: Who assesses property in Cedar Rapids?
faqs.a: The Cedar Rapids City Assessor does, from the City Services Center at 500 15th Avenue SW. The Linn County Assessor covers the rest of the county's real property.

faqs.q: When are Linn County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due September 1 and payable through September 30, and the second half is due March 1 and payable through March 31. Payments must be postmarked by those dates.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to protest a Linn County assessment?
faqs.a: April 30 of the assessment year, with filing opening April 2. Declared disaster areas get May 1 through June 5.

faqs.q: What late interest applies in Linn County?
faqs.a: Delinquent installments accrue interest of 1.5 percent per month, and the Treasurer notes a 1.5 percent late fee when a payment arrives without a valid postmark.

faqs.q: Where do I call the Linn County Treasurer?
faqs.a: 319-892-5500, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Phone hold times may be long, so a visit or an appointment at the Public Service Center can be faster.
